subject: IRS
category: An Appraisal of the Jahiliyyah Period and the Significance of the Islamic Reforms
question: Examine the nature and concept of idol worshipping in Arabia before Islam.
modelAnswer:
Nature and concept of idol worship in pre-Islamic Arabia (Jahiliyyah):
1. Origin: the Arabs were originally on the monotheism of Ibrahim and Isma'il, who built the Ka'bah. Tradition says 'Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i introduced idol worship, bringing the idol Hubal from Syria to Makkah.
2. Belief in Allah with intermediaries: they believed in Allah as the supreme Creator but worshipped idols as intercessors: 'We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah' (Q39:3; see also Q29:61).
3. Major idols: Hubal (in the Ka'bah, the chief idol of the Quraysh), al-Lat (at Ta'if), al-'Uzza (at Nakhlah, near Makkah) and Manat (at Qudayd, near Yathrib), regarded as 'daughters of Allah' (Q53:19–23). Older idols mentioned in the Qur'an include Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr (Q71:23).
4. Idols in the Ka'bah: about 360 idols were placed in and around the Ka'bah; the Prophet destroyed them at the conquest of Makkah in 630 CE, reciting 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished' (Q17:81).
5. Tribal and household idols: each tribe and many households had their own idols, which they touched for blessing before travelling.
6. Worship of natural objects: stones, trees (e.g. Dhat Anwat), stars, the sun and moon, and jinn (Q6:100).
7. Rituals: circumambulation of idols, sacrifices of animals on altars (nusub) to idols, vows and offerings of crops and cattle (Q6:136), and naked tawaf of the Ka'bah by some.
8. Divination: seeking decisions with divining arrows (azlam) before Hubal (Q5:3, 90), consulting soothsayers (kahin) and believing in omens.
9. A minority, the hunafa' (e.g. Zayd ibn 'Amr), rejected idol worship and held to the religion of Ibrahim; Jews and Christians also lived in Arabia.

Islam abolished idol worship and restored pure Tawhid.

subject: IRS
question: Give an account of the year of the Elephant.
modelAnswer:
The Year of the Elephant ('Am al-Fil), about 570 CE:
1. Abraha al-Ashram, the Abyssinian (Christian) ruler of Yemen under the king of Abyssinia, built a great church (al-Qullays) in San'a and wanted the Arabs to make pilgrimage to it instead of to the Ka'bah.
2. When an Arab defiled the church in protest, Abraha swore to destroy the Ka'bah and marched on Makkah with a large army and one or more elephants (the leading elephant is named Mahmud in the sources).
3. His men seized the camels of the Makkans, including two hundred belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's grandfather and leader of the Quraysh.
4. 'Abd al-Muttalib went to Abraha and asked only for his camels. When Abraha expressed surprise, he replied, 'I am the lord of the camels; the House has its own Lord who will protect it.'
5. The Quraysh withdrew to the hills around Makkah; 'Abd al-Muttalib prayed at the Ka'bah for Allah's protection.
6. When the army advanced, the elephant knelt and refused to move toward the Ka'bah, though it would move in other directions.
7. Allah sent flocks of birds (ababil) carrying stones of baked clay (sijjil), which they threw at the army; the soldiers were destroyed 'like eaten straw' (Surah al-Fil, Q105:1–5). Abraha was wounded and died on the way back to Yemen.

Significance:
1. The Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was born in that year.
2. It showed Allah's protection of the Ka'bah and prepared it as the centre of Islam.
3. It raised the prestige of the Quraysh among the Arabs as 'the people of Allah's House'.
4. The Arabs used it as a reference point for dating events.
5. It is recorded in Surah al-Fil as a sign of Allah's power.

subject: IRS
category: Life and Achievements of the Khulafa Rashidūn
question: Examine the circumstances that led to the assassination of Uthman bin Affan, the third caliph.
modelAnswer:
'Uthman ibn 'Affan was caliph from 644 to 656 CE (23–35 AH). Circumstances that led to his assassination:
1. Accusations of nepotism: he appointed many relatives from the Umayyad clan to high posts, e.g. Mu'awiyah in Syria, 'Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh in Egypt, al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah and later Sa'id ibn al-'As in Kufa, and his cousin Marwan ibn al-Hakam as secretary. Some of them behaved badly, e.g. al-Walid led prayer drunk.
2. Removal of respected companions from office, such as 'Amr ibn al-'As in Egypt and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in Kufa.
3. Financial grievances: he was accused of giving gifts from the treasury to relatives, though he was personally wealthy and generous.
4. Standardisation of the Qur'an: his order to burn other copies after the 'Uthmanic codex was compiled angered some reciters, though most companions approved.
5. Changes in practice, e.g. offering the full prayer at Mina, and the treatment of critics such as Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (sent to ar-Rabadhah), 'Ammar ibn Yasir and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.
6. Social and economic change: the conquests brought wealth and new converts; tension grew between the old Arab elite, the Quraysh and newly settled tribesmen in the garrison towns of Kufa, Basra and Fustat (Egypt).
7. Propaganda: agitators spread rumours against him; tradition names 'Abdullah ibn Saba' as an instigator, though historians debate his role.
8. The rebellion: in 35 AH groups of rebels from Egypt, Kufa and Basra came to Madinah with complaints. 'Uthman promised reforms and they left, but the Egyptians returned claiming they had found a letter, sealed with the caliph's seal, ordering their punishment (attributed by many to Marwan; 'Uthman denied writing it).
9. The siege: the rebels besieged his house for about forty days and cut off water. He refused to let the companions fight to defend him, to avoid shedding Muslim blood.
10. His death: the rebels broke in and killed him while he was reading the Qur'an, in Dhu al-Hijjah 35 AH (June 656 CE). His wife Na'ilah was injured trying to protect him.

Consequence: his assassination led to the first civil war (fitnah), the Battles of the Camel and Siffin, under 'Ali.
Note: the Khawarij emerged later, at the Battle of Siffin (657 CE), so they were not the group that killed 'Uthman.

subject: IRS
category: An Appraisal of the Jahiliyyah Period and the Significance of the Islamic Reforms
question: Enumerate and explain the functional administrative offices of the Kaabah before the advent of Islam.
modelAnswer:
Before Islam, the custodianship and services of the Ka'bah were organised as hereditary offices, mostly established by Qusayy ibn Kilab (the Prophet's ancestor), who gained control of Makkah from the Khuza'ah. The main offices were:
1. Hijabah (Sidanah): custody of the keys of the Ka'bah, opening and closing it, and looking after it. It later passed to the Banu 'Abd ad-Dar; after the conquest of Makkah the Prophet left the key with 'Uthman ibn Talhah of that clan.
2. Siqayah: providing drinking water for the pilgrims, later from the well of Zamzam; held by the Banu Hashim, then by al-'Abbas.
3. Rifadah: providing food for the pilgrims, funded by a tax on the Quraysh; held by Hashim, then 'Abd al-Muttalib, then Abu Talib.
4. Nadwah: presiding over Dar an-Nadwah, the council house where the Quraysh met to decide important matters (war, marriage, trade).
5. Liwa': holding the war banner (standard), tied and carried in war.
6. Qiyadah: command of the army in war; held by the Banu Umayyah (e.g. Abu Sufyan).
Other offices mentioned in some sources: Sifarah (acting as ambassador of the Quraysh, held by the Banu 'Adi, e.g. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab), Mashurah (advisory office), Ashnaq (fixing blood money and fines, held by Abu Bakr's clan, the Banu Taym), Qubbah and A'innah (the war tent and the reins of the horses, held by the Banu Makhzum) and the Azlam (keeping the divining arrows).

Significance: the offices gave the Quraysh clans prestige and authority among the Arabs and organised the pilgrimage, trade and defence of Makkah.

subject: IRS
category: The Conditions, Performance, and Performance of Hajj and Umrah
question: Enumerate what is permitted to Muhrim during Hajj exercise.
modelAnswer:
A muhrim is a pilgrim in the state of ihram for Hajj or 'Umrah. While many things are forbidden (e.g. sexual relations, perfume, cutting hair and nails, hunting, sewn clothes for men, covering the head for men, marriage contracts), the following are permitted:
1. Taking a bath (ghusl) or washing, including washing the head gently, for cleanliness or to cool off.
2. Changing the ihram garments for clean ones.
3. Seeking shade under a tent, umbrella, tree or the roof of a vehicle.
4. Wearing a belt, money pouch or bag, a ring, a watch or spectacles.
5. Wearing sandals (and khuffs if one cannot find sandals).
6. Gently scratching the head or body.
7. Cleaning the teeth with miswak.
8. Cupping (hijamah) and treating wounds, and taking unscented medicine.
9. Killing harmful creatures: the Prophet (SAW) allowed killing the crow, kite, scorpion, mouse and rabid (biting) dog (Bukhari and Muslim), and similar dangerous animals such as snakes.
10. Slaughtering and eating domestic animals (cattle, sheep, chickens).
11. Catching and eating sea game: 'Lawful to you is game from the sea' (Q5:96).
12. Looking in a mirror and wearing unscented clothing of any colour for women; women may wear their ordinary sewn clothes, socks and shoes, but should not wear the niqab or gloves.
13. Defending oneself and one's property.

Note: the schools of law (madhhabs) differ on some details, e.g. the use of unscented soap, combing the hair, and removing a broken nail; most allow removing a nail that is broken and causing pain.

subject: IRS
question: Examine the role of Hadith as a source of Islamic law.
modelAnswer:
Hadith (the reported sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet (SAW)) is the second source of Islamic law (Shari'ah) after the Qur'an.

Basis of its authority in the Qur'an:
1. 'Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it' (Q59:7).
2. 'Obey Allah and obey the Messenger' (Q4:59); 'He who obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah' (Q4:80).
3. 'Nor does he speak from his own desire; it is only a revelation revealed' (Q53:3–4).
4. 'We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to the people what was sent down to them' (Q16:44).
5. 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example' (Q33:21).

Roles of Hadith in Islamic law:
1. Confirming the Qur'an: it repeats and emphasises rulings already in the Qur'an (e.g. the obligation of prayer, fasting and honouring parents).
2. Explaining the Qur'an (bayan): it gives the details of acts commanded in general terms, e.g. the number of rak'ahs and method of prayer ('Pray as you have seen me pray', Bukhari), the rates of zakat, and the rites of Hajj ('Take your rites from me', Muslim).
3. Specifying general rulings (takhsis): e.g. the Qur'an gives children shares of inheritance, and the hadith specifies that a killer does not inherit from his victim.
4. Restricting unconditional rulings (taqyid): e.g. the Qur'an commands cutting the hand of a thief, and the hadith specifies the minimum value (nisab) and the wrist as the point of cutting.
5. Establishing new rulings not stated in the Qur'an: e.g. the prohibition of marrying a woman and her paternal or maternal aunt together, the prohibition of gold and silk for men, the rules of zakat al-fitr, and the stoning punishment for married adulterers according to the majority of jurists.
6. Providing the practical model of the Prophet's life (Sunnah) in worship, dealings and morals.
7. Serving as the basis of ijma' (consensus) and qiyas (analogy), the third and fourth sources of law.
8. Explaining the circumstances and meaning of verses (asbab an-nuzul).

Only authentic (sahih and hasan) hadith are used as proof in law, which is why the science of hadith criticism developed.

subject: IRS
question: Quote the quranic evidence on 'Wudu' and identify the obligatory aspects of 'Wudu'.
modelAnswer:
Qur'anic evidence (Q5:6):
'يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَاغْسِلُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ وَأَيْدِيَكُمْ إِلَى الْمَرَافِقِ وَامْسَحُوا بِرُءُوسِكُمْ وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ إِلَى الْكَعْبَيْنِ'
'O you who have believed, when you rise to perform prayer, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows, and wipe over your heads, and wash your feet to the ankles.'
The Prophet (SAW) also said, 'Allah does not accept the prayer of any of you who has broken wudu until he performs wudu' (Bukhari and Muslim).

Obligatory acts (fara'id) of wudu: according to the Maliki school, which is followed by most Muslims in Nigeria, there are seven:
1. Intention (niyyah) at the start of washing.
2. Washing the whole face, from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear.
3. Washing both arms up to and including the elbows.
4. Wiping (mash) the whole head.
5. Washing both feet up to and including the ankles.
6. Rubbing (dalk) the parts washed.
7. Continuity (muwalat / fawr): performing the acts without long interruption.

Note: the schools differ. The Shafi'i school lists six (intention, face, arms, wiping part of the head, feet, and doing them in order, tartib); the Hanafi school lists four (the four acts named in the verse: washing the face, washing the arms, wiping a quarter of the head and washing the feet). All schools agree on the four acts mentioned in the verse.

subject: IRS
category: The Observance, Types, and Values of Salāt
question: Examine the conditions for the authenticity of Salah (prayer).
modelAnswer:
The conditions for the validity (shurut as-sihhah) of salah, which must be fulfilled before and during the prayer:
1. Islam: the person praying must be a Muslim.
2. Sanity ('aql): prayer is not valid from an insane person.
3. Discernment (tamyiz) / maturity: a child is taught to pray from seven years and required from puberty.
4. Purity from ritual impurity (hadath): minor impurity is removed by wudu, major impurity (janabah, menstruation, post-natal bleeding) by ghusl, or tayammum when water is not available (Q5:6).
5. Purity of the body, clothes and place of prayer from filth (najasah): 'And your garments purify' (Q74:4).
6. Covering the 'awrah: for a man, from the navel to the knees; for a woman, the whole body except the face and hands (Q7:31).
7. Facing the Qiblah (the Ka'bah in Makkah): 'Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (Q2:144), except in fear or for voluntary prayer while riding.
8. Entry of the prayer time: 'Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times' (Q4:103).
9. Intention (niyyah) for the particular prayer; some scholars count it as a pillar (rukn) rather than a condition.
10. Freedom from menstruation and post-natal bleeding for women.

If any of these is missing, the prayer is not valid and must be repeated.
